usage: Doctor/nurse to patient; honorific 세요, the standard opener
반말; a parent to a child or between close friends
Softer, more formal clinic phrasing; 불편하다 = be uncomfortable
Where does it hurt the most?
Natural extension narrowing down the worst spot
examples: 어디가 아프세요? — 목이 아파요.
Where does it hurt? — My throat hurts.
The bare exchange the moment you sit down at the clinic
어디가 아프세요? 언제부터 그러셨어요?
Where does it hurt? Since when has it been like this?
Doctor pairs it with 'since when' to take a history
환자분, 어디가 아프세요? 천천히 말씀해 보세요.
Where does it hurt, sir/ma'am? Take your time and tell me.
Full clinic line; 환자분 = 'patient' as a respectful address
nuance: 어디가 아프세요? is the doctor's or nurse's standard polite opening to a patient, built from 어디가 'where (subject)' + 아프다 'to hurt' + honorific 세요. The patient does NOT say this to the doctor; the patient answers with a place + 아파요 (목이 아파요, 배가 아파요). Politeness shifts cleanly: 어디가 아파? is 반말 a parent uses with a child, and 어디가 불편하세요? is a gentler, slightly more formal version common at front desks. The classic English-speaker mistake is the particle: learners say 어디를 아프세요, but 아프다 is descriptive (an adjective-verb), so the hurting place is the SUBJECT and takes 가 — 어디가 아프세요?, never 어디를. Also note 아프다 covers both 'hurts' and 'is sick', so this one question opens almost every visit.

mistakes: Saying 어디를 아프세요? with the object particle 를.
아프다 is a descriptive verb, so the painful spot is the grammatical subject and takes 가/이. The correct form is 어디가 아프세요?
A patient using 어디가 아프세요? to the doctor.
This is the caregiver's question to the patient. As the patient you state the location yourself: 머리가 아파요 / 배가 아파요.
Translating 'what's wrong?' as 뭐가 틀렸어요?.
틀리다 means 'be wrong/incorrect' (as in an answer), not 'be ill'. For symptoms say 어디가 아프세요? or 어디가 불편하세요?

usage: 존댓말; describing your own symptom to a doctor
반말; telling a friend or family member
Formal 합쇼체; stiffer, e.g. reporting at a desk
I'm running a bit of a fever
Softer extension; 있어요 downplays it slightly
examples: 열이 나요. — 몇 도예요?
I have a fever. — What temperature?
The bare symptom and the natural follow-up question
어제부터 열이 나고 몸이 으슬으슬해요.
I've had a fever since yesterday and I feel chilly.
Everyday combo; 으슬으슬하다 = the shivery feeling of a fever
아이가 밤새 열이 나서 해열제를 먹였어요.
My child had a fever all night so I gave them fever medicine.
Parent to doctor; 해열제 = fever reducer, 먹이다 = make (someone) take
nuance: 열이 나요 is how you report a fever to a doctor, pharmacist, or anyone — literally 'heat comes out (열이 나다)'. Korean treats the fever as something that 'arises', so the natural verb is 나다, not 있다 or 하다; 열이 있어요 exists but sounds like 'there's some warmth', milder and more detached, while 열이 나요 is the everyday 'I'm running a fever'. The register shifts simply by ending: 열이 나 (반말) to a friend, 열이 나요 (존댓말) to a doctor, 열이 납니다 (격식) in formal speech. The big English-speaker error is 'I have a fever' → 열을 가지고 있어요 — a word-for-word calque with 가지다 'to possess' that no Korean says about symptoms; bodily states 'come' (나다) or 'exist' (있다), they are never 'had'. Also keep the particle 이: 열이 나요, not 열을 나요, because the fever is the subject of 나다.

mistakes: Saying 열을 가지고 있어요 for 'I have a fever'.
This literally translates English 'have' with 가지다 (to possess) and is unnatural for symptoms. Korean uses 열이 나요 ('a fever arises').
Using 열을 나요 with the object particle.
나다 ('to come out/arise') is intransitive, so 열 is the subject: 열이 나요, with 이, not 열을.
Saying 뜨거워요 to mean 'I have a fever'.
뜨겁다 describes a hot object you touch (hot coffee). Your body temperature being up is 열이 나요; 뜨거워요 about yourself sounds like your skin is burning hot to the touch.

usage: 존댓말; telling a doctor or pharmacist
반말; to a friend or family
Vivid extension for a severe headache
examples: 머리가 아파요. — 언제부터요?
I have a headache. — Since when?
Bare symptom plus the doctor's reflexive follow-up
아침부터 머리가 지끈지끈 아파요.
My head's been throbbing since this morning.
Everyday use; 지끈지끈 = the throbbing-ache mimetic
머리가 너무 아파서 회사를 조퇴했어요.
My head hurt so much I left work early.
Fuller situation; 조퇴하다 = leave work/school early
nuance: 머리가 아파요 is the go-to way to report any head pain — body-part + 가/이 + 아파요. The particle on the body part is the subject marker 가, because 아프다 is descriptive: the head is what 'is hurting', so it's the subject, never 머리를. This same frame builds every symptom: 배가 아파요, 목이 아파요, 이가 아파요. Register shifts by ending only (머리가 아파 / 아파요 / 아픕니다). Note 머리 means both 'head' and 'hair', so context decides; for the pain sense, 아파요 makes it unambiguous. English speakers often reach for the noun 'headache' and try 두통이 있어요 — that is correct and slightly more clinical (두통 = 頭痛, 'head-pain'), but in everyday speech 머리가 아파요 is far more common and natural; save 두통약 ('headache medicine') for the pharmacy counter.

아프다 is a descriptive verb, so the body part is the subject and takes 가/이: 머리가 아파요, not 머리를 아파요.
Saying 나는 머리 아파요 dropping the particle in formal speech.
Casual speech can drop 가, but to a doctor keep it: 머리가 아파요 sounds complete and clear, while bare 머리 아파 is 반말-flavored.
Using 두통해요 as a verb.
두통 is a noun; you can't verb it with 하다. Say 두통이 있어요 or, more naturally, 머리가 아파요.

usage: 반말; to family or a friend
Extension; 콕콕 쑤시다 = sharp, stabbing pains
examples: 배가 아파요. — 설사도 하세요?
My stomach hurts. — Do you also have diarrhea?
Bare symptom and the doctor's natural probe
어제 회를 먹고 나서 배가 아파요.
My stomach's been hurting since I ate raw fish yesterday.
Everyday cause-and-effect; 회 = raw fish (sashimi)
아침부터 배가 살살 아프더니 이제 너무 아파요.
It started as a mild ache this morning and now it really hurts.
Fuller progression; 살살 아프다 = ache gently/mildly
nuance: 배가 아파요 covers stomachache, bellyache, and cramps — 배 is the whole belly/abdomen, not just the stomach organ. Same descriptive frame as all symptoms: subject particle 가, never 배를. A key cultural note: 배가 아프다 also has an idiomatic meaning, 'to be jealous/envious' (literally 'my belly hurts' = it gnaws at me that someone else got something good), so 사촌이 땅을 사면 배가 아프다 is a proverb about envy — context makes the medical meaning clear at a clinic. To specify, Koreans add 윗배 (upper belly) or 아랫배 (lower belly). English speakers say 'stomach' and reach for 위(胃, the stomach organ), but 위가 아파요 sounds clinical and narrows it to the actual stomach; for a general bellyache always use 배가 아파요.

mistakes: Saying 배를 아파요 with the object particle.
아프다 is descriptive, so 배 is the subject: 배가 아파요, not 배를.
Using 위가 아파요 for a general bellyache.
위 is specifically the stomach organ and sounds clinical. For ordinary belly/abdominal pain say 배가 아파요.
Reading every 배가 아파요 as physical pain.
It can idiomatically mean 'I'm jealous'. At a clinic it's literal, but among friends 배 아파 ~ may tease 'I'm so envious', so let context decide.

usage: 존댓말; to a doctor or coworker
반말; to a friend, particle often dropped
I have come down with a cold
I feel a cold coming on
Extension for the early, mild stage
examples: 감기에 걸렸어요. — 약 드릴게요.
I caught a cold. — I'll get you some medicine.
Bare statement and the pharmacist's reply
애들한테 옮아서 감기에 걸렸어요.
I caught a cold from the kids.
Everyday context; 옮다 = catch/be infected (from someone)
독감인 줄 알았는데 그냥 감기에 걸린 거였어요.
I thought it was the flu, but it turned out to be just a cold.
Fuller situation contrasting 독감 (flu) with 감기 (cold)
nuance: 감기에 걸렸어요 is THE phrase for 'I caught a cold': 감기 'cold' + the location/target particle 에 + 걸리다 'to get caught/snagged' in the past. The fixed particle is 에, not 를 — you get 'caught ON/IN' the cold, like getting hooked, so 감기에 걸리다 is a set collocation; 감기를 걸렸어요 is wrong. Tense matters: 걸렸어요 (past) means you HAVE a cold now (you got caught and still are), which trips up English speakers who expect a present tense; 감기에 걸려요 sounds like a general habit ('I catch colds'). The dividing line with 독감 is severity: 감기 is a common cold, 독감 (毒感) is influenza, a different, harsher illness — don't call the flu 감기. For the very first signs, Koreans say 감기 기운이 있어요 ('there's a hint of a cold').

걸리다 here takes 에: 감기에 걸리다 is a fixed pairing. The object particle 를 is ungrammatical.
Using present 감기에 걸려요 to mean 'I have a cold now'.
걸리다 is the moment of catching it, so the past 걸렸어요 expresses the resulting state 'I have a cold'. Present tense sounds like a general tendency.
Calling the flu 감기.
감기 is a common cold; the flu is 독감. Mixing them up downplays a serious illness to a doctor.

usage: 반말; to a friend or family
examples: 기침이 나요. — 가래도 있어요?
I have a cough. — Any phlegm too?
Bare symptom and the doctor's follow-up; 가래 = phlegm
밤에 누우면 기침이 더 심해져요.
The cough gets worse when I lie down at night.
Everyday detail; 심해지다 = get more severe
기침이 2주째 안 멈춰서 엑스레이를 찍었어요.
I've been coughing for two weeks straight so they took an X-ray.
Fuller case; 2주째 = into the second week, 찍다 = take (an image)
nuance: 기침이 나요 reports a cough, again with 나다 ('to come out/arise') and the subject particle 이 — bodily phenomena 'arise' in Korean: 기침이 나다, 콧물이 나다, 열이 나다 all share this frame. You can also say 기침을 해요 ('I cough', 기침 + 하다), which emphasizes the action of coughing rather than its onset; the dividing line is subtle but 기침이 나요 = 'a cough is happening to me (a symptom)', while 기침을 해요 = 'I am coughing (doing it)'. Both are fine to a doctor. The English-speaker trap is, once more, treating it as a possession: 기침을 가지고 있어요 is a calque of 'I have a cough' and is wrong. Keep 이 with 나다 (not 기침을 나요), and reach for the partner symptom words 가래 (phlegm) and 콧물 (runny nose) that doctors will ask about next.

This calques English 'have'. Korean says 기침이 나요 or 기침을 해요.
Saying 기침을 나요 with 를 plus 나다.
나다 is intransitive, so 기침 is the subject: 기침이 나요. (If you want 를, the verb must be 하다: 기침을 해요.)
Confusing 기침 with 가래.
기침 is the cough; 가래 is the phlegm/mucus you cough up. The doctor asks 가래도 나요? as a separate question.

usage: 반말; particle often dropped with friends
Related extension for the opposite, a blocked nose
examples: 콧물이 나요. — 코도 막혔어요?
My nose is running. — Is it stuffy too?
Bare symptom and the natural paired question
재채기를 하면서 콧물이 계속 나요.
I keep sneezing and my nose won't stop running.
Everyday combo; 재채기 = a sneeze
환절기만 되면 콧물이 나고 눈이 가려워요.
Every change of season my nose runs and my eyes itch.
Fuller allergy picture; 환절기 = the turn-of-season period
nuance: 콧물이 나요 means 'my nose is running' — 콧물 is literally 'nose-water' (코 + 물, with the linking ㅅ giving 콧물), and again it 'arises' with 나다 + subject particle 이. Notice the contrast pair the doctor will probe: 콧물이 나요 (runny, wet nose) versus 코가 막혔어요 (blocked, stuffy nose) — opposite problems, different phrases, so don't blur them. English speakers calque 'runny nose' as an adjective and get stuck; Korean treats the mucus itself as the subject that comes out, so the literal logic is 'nose-water comes out'. Keep the particle 이 (콧물이 나요, not 콧물을 나요). In casual speech the particle drops (콧물 나), but to a doctor the full 콧물이 나요 is cleaner. Pair-words to know: 재채기 (sneeze), 가래 (phlegm), 콧물 (snot/runny nose).

나다 is intransitive; 콧물 is its subject, so 콧물이 나요, never 콧물을 나요.
Confusing 콧물이 나요 with 코가 막혔어요.
콧물이 나요 = a runny (wet) nose; 코가 막혔어요 = a blocked (stuffy) nose. They are opposite symptoms.
Writing 코물 instead of 콧물.
The compound 코 + 물 inserts a ㅅ받침: it is spelled 콧물 and pronounced [콘물]. 코물 is a spelling error.

english: I feel like I'm going to throw up
usage: 반말; to a friend or family
examples: 토할 것 같아요. — 봉투 여기 있어요.
I think I'm going to be sick. — Here's a bag.
Bare warning and a quick practical response
차만 타면 멀미가 나서 토할 것 같아요.
I get carsick the moment I'm in a car and feel like throwing up.
Everyday cause; 멀미가 나다 = get motion sickness
어지럽고 속이 울렁거려서 진짜 토할 것 같아요.
I'm dizzy and my stomach is churning, I really feel like I'll throw up.
Fuller state; 울렁거리다 = (stomach) churn/heave
nuance: 토할 것 같아요 = 토하다 'to vomit' + 을 것 같다 'it seems like / I feel like (it will happen)', so 'I feel like I'm about to throw up'. The 을 것 같다 frame is essential: it expresses an impending sensation, not a completed act, which is exactly what you want to warn a nurse before it happens. The blunter verb 토하다 is fine medically but graphic in polite small talk; gentler options are 속이 안 좋아요 ('my stomach's off'), 메스꺼워요/울렁거려요 ('I feel queasy') — the dividing line is intensity, with 토할 것 같아요 being the urgent one. English speakers misuse 같아요 as a hedge meaning 'I think' and attach it loosely; here it's bound to the 을 것 form (토할 것 같아요), so don't say 토해요 같아요. Also avoid the casual 게워요 with strangers — it's colloquial; 토하다 is the neutral verb.

mistakes: Saying 토해요 같아요 to mean 'I feel like throwing up'.
같다 must attach to the 을 것 form: 토할 것 같아요. You can't bolt 같아요 onto a finished verb.
Using 토할 것 같아요 only after you've already vomited.
The 을 것 같다 frame is for an impending feeling. If it already happened, say 토했어요.
Saying 던지다 because a dictionary glosses 'throw up' as 'throw'.
던지다 means physically throw an object. 'Throw up' (vomit) is 토하다 — a completely different verb.

usage: 반말; to a friend or family
Vivid colloquial extension; 핑 돌다 = go light-headed/spin
examples: 어지러워요. — 앉으세요.
I feel dizzy. — Please sit down.
Bare symptom and an immediate caring response
갑자기 일어나면 어지러워요.
I get dizzy when I stand up suddenly.
Everyday trigger; 갑자기 = suddenly, 일어나다 = stand up
며칠째 어지럽고 속이 메스꺼워서 병원에 왔어요.
I've been dizzy and nauseous for a few days so I came to the clinic.
Fuller reason for the visit; 며칠째 = for several days running
nuance: 어지러워요 means 'I feel dizzy/light-headed'. The base is the ㅂ-irregular adjective 어지럽다, which conjugates 어지럽다 → 어지러워요 (the ㅂ turns to 우/워), a spelling point learners stumble on. As a descriptive verb of state it stands alone — no body-part subject needed, unlike 머리가 아파요. The near-neighbor 현기증이 나요 ('I have vertigo', 현기증 = 眩氣症) is more clinical and names the symptom as a noun that 'arises' with 나다; the dividing line is everyday 어지러워요 vs. medical 현기증이 나요. English speakers regularize the ㅂ-irregular to 어지럽어요 — wrong; it must be 어지러워요. Another slip is reaching for 미쳐요 ('go crazy/spin') from 'my head is spinning'; that means losing your mind, not feeling faint. For light-headedness on standing, 어지러워요 is exactly right.

mistakes: Saying 어지럽어요 by regularizing the verb.
어지럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: the ㅂ becomes 워 before 어요, giving 어지러워요, not 어지럽어요.
Saying 머리가 어지러워요.
어지럽다 already describes your whole head/state, so a body-part subject is redundant. Just say 어지러워요.
Using 미쳐요 for 'my head is spinning'.
미치다 = go crazy/insane. Dizziness is 어지러워요 or 현기증이 나요; 미쳐요 has nothing to do with feeling faint.

usage: 반말; only with very close people, rare here
Could you give me the prescription, please?
More formal, polite request with 시겠어요
examples: 처방전 주세요. — 여기 있습니다.
The prescription, please. — Here you go.
Bare request and the staff's reply at the desk
약국에 가야 하니까 처방전 주세요.
I need to go to the pharmacy, so please give me the prescription.
Everyday reason; the doctor's office issues it, the 약국 fills it
전에 받은 처방전을 잃어버렸는데 다시 발급해 주세요.
I lost the prescription I got before; please reissue it.
Fuller situation; 잃어버리다 = lose, 발급 = issuance
nuance: 처방전 주세요 asks for the prescription slip — 처방전 (處方箋, 'prescription document') + 주세요 'please give'. In Korea the system is split: the doctor (병원/의원) writes the 처방전, and you take it to a separate pharmacy (약국) to get the actual medicine — so you literally receive a paper (increasingly sent electronically) to hand over. Don't confuse 처방전 (the slip) with 처방 (the act of prescribing) or with 약 (the medicine itself). 주세요 is the standard polite 'give me'; to be softer use 주시겠어요? or 주실 수 있어요?. The English-speaker confusion is expecting the doctor to hand over pills directly, so they ask for 약 at the clinic — but at the 병원 you ask for the 처방전, and at the 약국 you ask them to fill it (약 지어 주세요). Saying 처방전 주세요 to the pharmacist is backwards; you GIVE the slip there.

You HAND the 처방전 to the pharmacist, you don't receive it there. At the 약국 say 약 지어 주세요 or hand over the slip.
Saying 처방 주세요 instead of 처방전.
처방 is the act of prescribing; the physical slip is 처방전. Drop the 전 and it sounds incomplete.

english: Could you fill this prescription / make up the medicine?
usage: Please make up the medicine for me
존댓말; patient to pharmacist, 좀 softens it
반말; rare in a pharmacy, used jokingly with close people
Could you make up the medicine, please?
More polite request form with 주시겠어요
Please fill this exactly as prescribed
Extension handing over the slip; 처방전대로 = as per the prescription
examples: 약 좀 지어 주세요. — 처방전 주시겠어요?
Could you fill this? — May I have the prescription?
Bare request and the pharmacist's standard reply
감기약 좀 지어 주세요. 콧물이랑 기침이 심해요.
Please make up some cold medicine. My runny nose and cough are bad.
Everyday over-the-counter request describing symptoms
아이가 먹을 거라서 가루약으로 약 좀 지어 주세요.
It's for my child, so please make it up as powder medicine.
Fuller request; 가루약 = powdered medicine, easier for kids
nuance: 약 좀 지어 주세요 is what you say to a pharmacist: 약 'medicine' + 짓다 'to make/compose' + 주세요 'please (for me)'. The verb 짓다 is special — it's the same 'build/compose' used for 밥을 짓다 (cook rice) and 집을 짓다 (build a house); medicine is 'composed/made up', reflecting the traditional pharmacy that measures and combines doses. Note 짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular: 짓다 → 지어 (the ㅅ drops), so it's 지어 주세요, not 짓어 주세요. 좀 ('a bit') is the politeness softener that turns a bare order into a friendly request. The dividing line from 약 주세요 ('give me medicine') is that 지어 주세요 implies preparing/compounding from a prescription or for your symptoms, while 약 주세요 just means hand over a ready product. English speakers calque 'fill a prescription' with 채우다 ('to fill (a container)') — completely wrong here; the idiom is 약을 짓다.

짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ drops before 어, giving 지어. So it's 약 지어 주세요.
Using 채우다 to translate 'fill a prescription'.
채우다 means fill a physical container. 'Make up medicine' is 약을 짓다 — 약 지어 주세요.

Without 좀 and with 반말 it sounds like a brusque order. To a pharmacist use 약 좀 지어 주세요.

english: Take it three times a day
usage: Take it three times a day
Take it three times a day
반말; a parent telling a child
하루 세 번, 한 알씩 드세요
Take one tablet, three times a day
Extension adding the dose; 한 알씩 = one tablet each
examples: 하루 세 번 드세요. — 네, 알겠습니다.
Take it three times a day. — Okay, got it.
Bare instruction and the patient's acknowledgment
이 약은 하루 세 번, 식후에 드세요.
Take this three times a day, after meals.
Everyday full instruction; 식후 = after eating
증상이 없어져도 하루 세 번 끝까지 다 드세요.
Even if symptoms go, take it three times a day to the end.
Fuller advice (e.g. antibiotics); 끝까지 = all the way through
nuance: 하루 세 번 드세요 is the dosing instruction you'll hear constantly: 하루 'a day' + 세 번 'three times' + 드세요, the honorific imperative of 먹다 'to take/eat'. Crucial counting point — 번 ('times/occurrences') takes NATIVE Korean numbers in their counter form: 한 번, 두 번, 세 번, 네 번, so 'three times' is 세 번, never the Sino-Korean 삼 번. The verb to a patient is the honorific 드세요 (or clinical 복용하세요), while 먹어 is 반말 to a child. The English-speaker error is the number system: learners say 삼 번 by analogy with reading numbers aloud, but with the counter 번 you need native 세 번. Another slip is word order — Korean is 하루 세 번 ('day three times'), the opposite of English 'three times a day'; the time unit comes first. Pair it with 식후 (after meals) or 식전 (before meals) for the full instruction.

Putting it in English order: 세 번 하루.
Korean states the larger time unit first: 하루 세 번 ('a day, three times'), not 세 번 하루.
Using 먹으세요 vs 드세요 incorrectly to an elder patient.
To a patient the honorific 드세요 (or 복용하세요) is the norm; 먹어 is 반말 for a child. Plain 먹으세요 is acceptable but 드세요 is more polite.

english: Take it thirty minutes after meals
usage: 밥 먹고 삼십 분 뒤에 먹어
Eat, then take it 30 minutes later
반말; plainer wording to a child/friend
examples: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. — 네.
Take it 30 minutes after meals. — Okay.
The bare instruction printed on most Korean medicine bags
속 쓰릴 수 있으니까 꼭 식후 삼십 분에 드세요.
It can upset your stomach, so be sure to take it 30 minutes after eating.
Everyday reasoning; 속 쓰리다 = have an acidy/burning stomach
이건 식전, 저건 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. 헷갈리지 마세요.
Take this before meals and that one 30 minutes after; don't mix them up.
Fuller two-medicine instruction; 헷갈리다 = get confused/mixed up
nuance: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 — literally '식후 (食後, after-meal) 삼십 분 (30 minutes) 에 (at) take' — is the timing line on almost every Korean prescription bag (약봉투). Note the number system flips here versus 번: time durations and Sino-Korean compounds use SINO numbers, so '30 minutes' is 삼십 분, and the particle 에 marks the point in time ('at 30 minutes after'). Learn the set: 식전 (before meals), 식후 (after meals), 식간 (between meals), 취침 전 (before bed). The contrast that matters is 식전 vs 식후 — taking a 식후 drug on an empty stomach can cause 속 쓰림 (stomach burning), so the distinction is medically real, not just vocabulary. English speakers mix the number systems (saying 세십 분 or using 분 with native numbers) and drop the time particle 에; keep it as 삼십 분에. Also don't translate 'after meals' as 식사 후에 only — 식후 is the compact written norm on labels.

Clock/duration minutes use Sino-Korean numerals: 삼십 분, not native 서른 분.
Dropping the time particle 에: 식후 삼십 분 드세요.
The point in time needs 에: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. Without it the timing relation is unclear.
Confusing 식전 and 식후.
식전 = before meals, 식후 = after meals. They are opposites, and the wrong one can upset your stomach.

usage: 반말; asking a friend who might have some
Softer, gentler polite question with 나요
Extension moving from asking to requesting
examples: 진통제 있어요? — 네, 어떤 통증이세요?
Do you have painkillers? — Yes, what kind of pain?
Bare question and the pharmacist's natural probe
생리통이 심한데 진통제 있어요?
My period cramps are bad — do you have painkillers?
Everyday context; 생리통 = menstrual pain
타이레놀 같은 진통제 있어요? 두통이 너무 심해서요.
Do you have a painkiller like Tylenol? My headache is really bad.
Fuller request naming a brand; 같은 = like/such as
nuance: 진통제 있어요? asks the pharmacist whether they stock painkillers — 진통제 (鎭痛劑, 'pain-suppress agent') + 있어요? 'is there?/do you have?'. 있어요? is the everyday polite way to ask about availability of any product, far more natural than a textbook 가지고 있어요?. Good vocabulary to pair: 두통약 (headache medicine), 소화제 (digestive aid), 해열제 (fever reducer), 소염제 (anti-inflammatory) — Korean names many drugs by the symptom + 제/약. The dividing line: 진통제 is the general painkiller category, while naming a brand (타이레놀) or a specific use (생리통약, period-pain medicine) narrows it. English speakers calque 'do you have' with 가지고 있어요?, which sounds like asking if the pharmacist personally carries one on them; for shop stock always use 있어요?. Also note painkillers like ibuprofen are sold over the counter (일반의약품) without a prescription, so this question is genuinely useful.

가지고 있다 = personally possess. To ask whether a store stocks something, use 있어요?: 진통제 있어요?

There is no 아픔약. The word is 진통제, or by symptom e.g. 두통약 (headache medicine).

진통제 relieves pain; 해열제 reduces fever. They overlap in some products but ask for the right one.

english: If it's really bad, go see a doctor
usage: If it gets bad, go to the doctor
If it's bad, go to the doctor
반말; to a friend or younger family member
많이 안 좋으시면 병원에 가 보세요
If you feel worse, do see a doctor
More polite; subject honorific 좋으시면 + 가 보세요
If it doesn't improve, go to the doctor
Extension; 차도가 없다 = show no improvement
examples: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요. — 네, 그럴게요.
If it's bad, go see a doctor. — Okay, I will.
Bare advice and the customer's agreement
이 약 먹고도 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요.
If you're still bad after this medicine, go to the doctor.
Everyday pharmacist follow-up; 먹고도 = even after taking
며칠 지켜보다가 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요. 그냥 감기가 아닐 수도 있어요.
Watch it for a few days, and if it's bad, see a doctor — it might not be just a cold.
Fuller advice; 지켜보다 = keep an eye on, ~일 수도 있다 = might be
nuance: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 is the kindly send-off a pharmacist gives: 많이 'a lot' + 안 좋으면 'if (it's) not good' (the conditional ~으면) + 병원 가세요 'go to the hospital/clinic'. Two cultural points. First, 병원 in Korea means any medical facility from a tiny neighborhood clinic (의원) up to a big hospital — 'go to 병원' just means 'see a doctor', not necessarily a hospital admission, which surprises English speakers. Second, 안 좋다 ('not good') is the gentle, idiomatic way to say a symptom is worsening; it's softer than 나빠지면 ('if it gets bad') and very natural. To be more polite, add the subject honorific: 많이 안 좋으시면 가 보세요, where 가 보세요 ('try going') is gentler than a flat 가세요. English speakers literally translate 'go to the hospital' and picture an ER; here it routinely means a regular clinic visit. Keep the conditional 으면 attached to 좋다 (안 좋으면), not a separate 만약 clause alone.

병원 covers clinics too; it simply means 'see a doctor'. For admission you'd say 입원하다.
Saying 만약 안 좋다 병원 가세요 without the conditional ending.
'If' needs the ~으면 ending on the verb: 안 좋으면. 만약 is optional emphasis, not a replacement for 으면.
Using 나쁘면 instead of 안 좋으면 about how you feel.
For health, the idiomatic 'if you feel worse' is 안 좋으면. 나쁘다 about a person can sound like 'bad-natured'; 몸이 안 좋다 is the set phrase for feeling unwell.

english: I'm aching all over / I'm run down
usage: 반말; particle often dropped with friends
I feel run-down, like a body ache coming on
examples: 몸살이 났어요. — 푹 쉬세요.
I ache all over. — Get plenty of rest.
Bare symptom and the caring reply; 푹 쉬다 = rest fully
무리해서 일했더니 몸살이 났어요.
I overdid it at work and now I'm aching all over.
Everyday cause; 무리하다 = overexert oneself
감기 끝에 몸살이 나서 온몸이 쑤시고 기운이 없어요.
After the cold I came down achy, my whole body throbs and I have no energy.
Fuller state; 온몸이 쑤시다 = the whole body aches, 기운이 없다 = feel drained
nuance: 몸살이 났어요 has no clean English equivalent: 몸살 is the run-down, achy-all-over, feverish-exhaustion state you get from overwork or a cold — body aches plus fatigue. It pairs with 나다 ('arise') in the past, 몸살이 났어요, meaning you've come down with it. Don't confuse 몸살 (body aches/exhaustion) with 감기 (a cold) — they often come together (감기몸살) but 몸살 specifically is the muscle-aching, drained feeling, while 감기 is the respiratory cold (runny nose, cough). The cause is typically overexertion (무리하다), so Koreans say 몸살 났어 after a hard week. English speakers have no word for this and try to describe it piecemeal ('I'm tired and my body hurts'); learning 몸살이 났어요 captures it in one phrase. Keep the subject particle 이 (몸살이 났어요) and the past tense for the resulting state, like 감기에 걸렸어요.

mistakes: Treating 몸살 as the same as 감기.
감기 is a respiratory cold; 몸살 is the body-ache/exhaustion state. They co-occur (감기몸살) but aren't identical.
Saying 몸살을 했어요 with 를 + 하다.
The collocation is 몸살이 나다: 몸살이 났어요. It 'arises', it isn't 'done'.
Using present 몸살이 나요 for a current case.
Like 감기에 걸렸어요, the past 몸살이 났어요 expresses the present state of having it. Present tense sounds like a general tendency.

usage: Do I have to get a shot?
Do I have to get a shot?
반말; a child to a parent
주사 안 맞고 약만 먹으면 안 돼요?
Can't I just take pills instead of a shot?
examples: 주사 맞아야 해요? — 아니요, 약만 드시면 돼요.
Do I need a shot? — No, just take the medicine.
Bare question and a reassuring answer
독감 예방 주사 맞아야 해요?
Should I get the flu vaccine shot?
Everyday preventive context; 예방 주사 = vaccination/preventive shot
열이 안 떨어지는데 주사 맞아야 해요? 주사는 좀 무서워서요.
My fever won't break — do I need a shot? I'm a bit scared of needles.
Fuller exchange; 열이 떨어지다 = fever comes down
nuance: 주사 맞아야 해요? asks whether you need an injection — and the verb is the surprise: you 'receive/are hit by' a shot, 주사를 맞다, using 맞다 ('to be struck/get hit'), NOT 주사를 하다 or 주사를 받다. So 'get a shot' = 주사 맞다, 'get a vaccine' = 예방 주사 맞다. The ~아야 하다 frame means 'have to/must', so 맞아야 해요? = 'do I have to get (a shot)?'. In casual speech 해요 becomes 돼요 (맞아야 돼요?), both fine. The English-speaker error is almost universal here: calquing 'get/receive a shot' as 주사를 받다 (받다 = receive a thing handed to you) — wrong; injections are 맞다. Likewise 주사를 하다 ('do a shot') is what the nurse does to you, not what you say as the patient. 주사 itself (注射) covers both the injection and the needle. Pair it with 약만 먹으면 돼요? to ask for the pill alternative.

mistakes: Saying 주사를 받아야 해요 with 받다.
받다 = receive a handed object. An injection uses 맞다 ('be struck'): 주사 맞아야 해요?
Saying 주사를 해야 해요 as the patient.
주사를 하다 is what the medical staff does (administers). As the one getting it, you say 주사를 맞다.
Confusing 맞다 'be hit' here with 맞다 'be correct'.
Same spelling, but 주사를 맞다 specifically means 'get an injection'. Context (주사) makes it the shot meaning.
